title: a year of service designed
hook: the Gita sorts gifts into three kinds, and only one needs no thank-you
carry: why, what back, when, to whom

segments.voice: Yesterday, piece two of a year of service: svadharma, better your own service, done imperfectly, than someone else's done well.

A twenty-dollar bill can be three completely different gifts. Handed over with a little speech about how generous this is. Pushed across the table with a sigh, because saying no would be awkward. Or slipped to the right person, at the right moment, with no one keeping score. Same bill. Chapter seventeen of the Gita would say those aren't the same act at all. Krishna sorts faith, food, sacrifice and discipline there by the three gunas, the three qualities that run through everything, and giving gets its own three verses.
screen: `ONE BILL, THREE GIFTS.` → `CHAPTER SEVENTEEN SORTS THEM.` → `HOW TO GIVE.`

segments.voice: The gunas are sattva, clarity and balance; rajas, restless drive; and tamas, heaviness and dullness. Here are the three gifts, in paraphrase. The sattvic gift is given simply because giving is right, to someone who can do nothing in return, at the right place and time, to a fitting person. The rajasic gift is given to get something back, or with an eye to some reward, or grudgingly. The tamasic gift is given at the wrong place and time, to the wrong person, without respect, with contempt. Look at what the first gift asks for. Not size; the verse doesn't mention an amount at all. Four things: the right reason, which is that it's right; no return; the right timing; and the right person. That last part keeps it from being careless. Giving well takes attention. Who actually needs this? Is now the moment, or would next month be better for them? The second gift isn't evil. It's just tangled up with getting, and the Gita puts giving with reluctance in it, which is honest about how giving can feel. The third comes with contempt, so whatever it helps with, it also wounds. For a year of service, this is the money and things part of the plan. Before you decide what to give, the Gita would have you ask four questions. Why am I giving? What am I expecting back? When is the right time? To whom? Dana, the gift, is part of Hindu practice. Chapter seventeen asks that it be done with clear eyes.
screen: `THREE GUNAS, THREE GIFTS.` · `SATTVIC: RIGHT, NO RETURN, RIGHT TIME, RIGHT PERSON.` · `RAJASIC: TO GET BACK, OR GRUDGING.` · `TAMASIC: WITH CONTEMPT.` · then, large: `GIVE WITH CLEAR EYES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one gift you've given recently, money, time, a favor, a meal, and hold it up to the four questions gently, without scoring yourself: why, what back, when, to whom. Then picture one gift you might give in the coming weeks, ask the same four questions, and see if any answer shifts. If you pray, you can offer that future gift to the one you pray to before it's given.
Dana. The gift, given because it's right, with nothing expected back, at the right time, to the right person.
Your line: why, what back, when, to whom. Not one of the four asks how much. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 971 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A YEAR OF SERVICE DESIGNED.`

howItsDone: Dana, giving, is part of Hindu practice at festivals, temple visits and family occasions, and some Hindus point to the Gita's description of the sattvic gift, given without expecting return, when they talk about how to give.

fork.setup: you want to give, and you want it to count as the Gita's sattvic gift. what matters most?
options: that it's large enough to be noticed.
that it's given because it's right, expecting nothing, to the right person at the right time.
that the person knows exactly who gave it.
fork.reveal: Gita 17.20 names no amount. It asks for the right reason, no return, the right place and time, and a fitting person.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: dana, the gift or giving. Gita 17.20–22 sorts it by the three gunas.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gift is a gift; it only matters how much.
what it means: the Gita sorts gifts by why, when, to whom, and whether anything is expected back.
what a scholar hears: Gita 17.20–22, part of chapter seventeen's sorting of faith, food, sacrifice, austerity and giving by sattva, rajas and tamas.
recall: barley flour, the poor family's whole gift
a thread tied as a promise of care

chat.says: Does the Gita say the best gift is the biggest one?
options: No, it skips amount: it's given because it's right, expecting nothing back.
Yes, the more you give, the more sattvic the gift becomes, however it's given.
No, the best gift is one given grudgingly, since it costs you more.
chat.meaning: The sattvic gift in chapter seventeen asks for the right reason, no return, the right time and the right person. It never mentions an amount.
